JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR          §                         BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY           §
LLC AND LCRA TSC TO AMEND           §                                        OF
THEIR CERTIFICATES OF               §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY           §                         ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST            §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL                  §
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE §
IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,   §
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,             §
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, §
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,    §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES             §

      SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS OF COMMISSION STAFF
      AND APPLICANTS REGARDING NEED FOR IMPORT PATH 2 PROJECTS

                                      I.     INTRODUCTION

       SWG Briggs I, L.P. (“SWG Briggs”) respectfully files this Reply to the Exceptions filed

by Commission Staff and by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

Service Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) on September 2, 2026, concerning the Proposal

for Decision (“PFD”) issued by the State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”)

Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) on August 20, 2026.

       The PFD correctly found that Applicants failed to establish that the Import Path 2 Projects

are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public under Public

Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.056. The ALJs’ conclusion rests on four independent

grounds: (1) Applicants did not present a case for the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart

from the three 765-kV import paths as one comprehensive project; (2) changed circumstances

mean that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan’s (“PBRP”) underlying projected loads do not

support the Projects and should be re-evaluated; (3) Applicants failed to prove that sufficient power




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                       1
 is available at Bell County East to transmit westward via Import Path 2; and (4) intervenors

submitted credible evidence of generation alternatives—new and planned gas generation in the

Permian Basin—that could reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2. See PFD at 98-99.

These independent findings confirm that the record does not support approving the Applications.

       Commission Staff’s and Applicants’ Exceptions are meritless. They ask the Commission

to afford dispositive weight to ERCOT’s recommendation while disregarding material changes in

circumstances that have undermined the PBRP’s foundational assumptions, to approve a multi-

billion-dollar transmission project without requiring Applicants to demonstrate that the proposed

facilities will actually perform their asserted function, and to dismiss the significant body of

evidence demonstrating that the PBRP’s planning process was fundamentally flawed. For the

reasons set forth below, the Exceptions should be denied and the PFD’s findings on need should

be sustained.

      II.       THE PFD CORRECTLY CONCLUDED THAT APPLICANTS FAILED TO
                                   ESTABLISH NEED

   A. The “Great Weight” Standard Does Not Relieve Applicants of Their Burden to Prove
      Need

       Commission Staff and Applicants contend that the Commission’s rule requiring “great

weight” be afforded to ERCOT’s recommendation for reliability projects under 16 TEX. ADMIN.

CODE § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) is essentially dispositive of the need determination. But “great

weight” is not synonymous with automatic deference. The rule conditions great weight on

projected load growth being “substantiated by quantifiable evidence.” 16 TEX. ADMIN. CODE §

25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). The Commission retains an independent obligation under PURA § 37.056

to determine whether an applicant has demonstrated that proposed transmission facilities are




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                   2
 “necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” See TEX. UTIL.

CODE § 37.056(a).

       The PFD identified two specific reasons why ERCOT’s recommendation should not

receive great weight. First, ERCOT’s reliability recommendation relies on a non-oil-and-gas load

forecast in which 55% of the PBRP’s projected non-oil-and-gas load was confirmed only by a

transmission-service-provider officer letter and another 6% was unconfirmed; ERCOT’s own 2025

realization-rate methodology would materially reduce those projections, cutting the forecasted

non-oil-and-gas load by at least 3,571 MW—an amount material in relation to Import Path 2’s

5,270-MW safe loading limit. See PFD at 90-91; Proposed FOFs 87-95, 132-140. Second,

ERCOT’s recommendation was based on the S&P Global study, which ERCOT did not verify or

independently evaluate, and for which ERCOT made no credibility finding. ERCOT stated it was

“required by statute” to use the study, but that statutory compliance does not constitute

endorsement of S&P Global’s forecasts. See PFD at 91-92; Proposed FOFs 136-140. The PFD

further found that the weight of the PBRP was undermined by the lack of robust stakeholder input:

only 17 entities and the Applicants submitted formal comments, and the plan was not subject to

additional ERCOT Regional Planning Group (“RPG”) review before CCN applications could be

filed. See PFD at 92-93; Proposed FOFs 82-84.

   B. Changed Circumstances Undermine the PBRP’s Load Forecasts and the Asserted
      Need

       Applicants argue that “changed circumstances” actually “affirm rather than undermine” the

need for Import Path 2. The record contradicts that assertion. The PFD found that ERCOT’s

adjusted methodology for the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan (“RTP”) reduced officer-letter-

confirmed load to 55.4% and data-center load to 49.8% of submitted amounts, with a combined

27.6% rate for data-center load confirmed by an officer letter. See PFD at 63. Applying that



SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                   3
 methodology to the PBRP’s non-oil-and-gas projections “would result in a material reduction to

the forecasted non-oil and gas load of at least 3,571 MW”—a significant portion of Import Path

2’s 5,270-MW safe loading limit—and the PBRP forecast has not been retested against that

methodology. See PFD at 74-75; Proposed FOFs 87-93.

       Regarding oil-and-gas load, the PFD found the S&P Global study—the sole study used by

ERCOT for the PBRP’s oil-and-gas load forecast—was prepared for major oil-and-gas companies

and submitted to ERCOT by Oncor. See PFD at 58. The PFD identified serious methodological

problems: S&P Global “built its projections on surveys of unconstrained ‘wish list’ scenarios and

corporate pledges,” and its core premise—that Permian Basin producers had to electrify to reduce

greenhouse-gas profiles—“has been proven incorrect by S&P Global’s own later analysis,” which

showed absolute greenhouse-gas emissions declined 20% between 2022 and 2025 even as

production increased by approximately 500,000 barrels per day. See PFD at 80-81; Proposed FOFs

104-109. ERCOT’s latest forecast projects 3.1 GW of new oil-and-gas load by 2030, compared

with S&P Global’s 10.3 GW projection; the 2025 RTP identifies oil-and-gas load as only 7% of

system-wide large-load growth. See PFD at 80-81; Proposed FOF 109.

       The non-oil-and-gas load mix has likewise shifted materially. The PBRP projected that

59% of its non-oil-and-gas load—approximately 6,900 MW—would serve cryptocurrency mining.

By the 2025 RTP, non-crypto data centers constituted 55% of system-wide large-load growth while

crypto constituted only 9%. As the PFD found, “a project designed to serve 6,900 MW of crypto

load is not automatically the correct project to serve a materially different load mix of equivalent

nominal size.” See PFD at 75; Proposed FOF 95. Senate Bill 6’s new credibility standards and

Commission’s June 18, 2026 Batch Zero process further confirm that large-load forecasts require

current review. See PFD at 76-77; Proposed FOFs 96-101. Applicants’ own witness Jared Gurley




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                      4
 admitted that Applicants did not verify the officer-letter load, while Staff witness John Poole

acknowledged that a re-evaluation of forecasted demand is warranted. See PFD at 74, 76; Proposed

FOF 100.

   C. The Far West Texas Import Generic Transmission Constraints (“GTCs”) Do Not
      Independently Establish Need

       Applicants and Commission Staff argue that the Far West Texas Import GTCs provide a

separate, present-day reliability basis for Import Path 2. The PFD properly rejected this argument,

finding that the GTCs “have not resulted in any load shed to date” and that “the price-

responsiveness of crypto-miners and charging/discharging behavior of batteries have provided

some operating margin during constrained conditions.” See PFD at 82-83; Proposed FOFs 112-

116. The 765-kV import paths are only one of seven transmission upgrades ERCOT identifies to

“help” exit the GTCs. As the PFD correctly found, “GTCs measure transmission system

constraints; they do not validate the composition or reliability of the load on the demand side,” and

a “GTC driven substantially by speculative cryptocurrency mining load is not the same as a GTC

driven by stable industrial or residential load.” See PFD at 83; Proposed FOFs 114-116. Applicants

have not separated the load driving the GTCs from the speculative load that undermines the PBRP

forecast; the GTCs therefore cannot independently cure the deficiencies in those forecasts.

   D. Applicants Failed to Demonstrate That Import Path 2 Can Perform Its Asserted
      Function

       The PFD found that Import Path 2 is intended to bring power into the Permian Basin, not

export it, and identified reliability concerns and supply constraints in the Central Texas Corridor.

The 2025 RTP states that “Central Texas faces the challenge of needing additional import

capability” and existing paths “currently consist of lower-rated 345-kV lines which limit the power

transfer capability into the area.” See PFD at 84-85; Proposed FOFs 117-120. Former Commission




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                       5
 Chairman Smitherman testified, “I am not aware of any similar announcement for generation

capacity at or near the Bell County East proposed substation.” See PFD at 85.

       Applicants did not identify specific generation resources expected to import power into the

Permian Basin via Import Path 2, did not prove that sufficient power is available at Bell County

East to transmit westward, and admitted that no sensitivity analysis was performed on project

viability if the Central Texas generation base proves insufficient to serve both local load and the

export function. See Proposed FOFs 121-127. The PFD concluded: “A 765-kV transmission line

authorized to transmit bulk power into the Permian Basin cannot be shown to be needed for

reliability when the record establishes that the analysis of whether the grid can actually deliver that

reliability has not been done.” See PFD at 85.

   E. Generation Alternatives Were Not Adequately Evaluated

       The PFD identified 24 natural-gas generation projects in the Permian Basin totaling 25.162

GW: one under construction (1.35 GW), 16 in pre-construction (15.627 GW), and seven

announced (8.115 GW). See PFD at 95. ERCOT’s latest 2030 forecast for the Far West region is

17 GW, meaning planned generation rivals or exceeds the PBRP’s projected load. See id.; Proposed

FOFs 141-145. These include Competitive Power Ventures’ Basin Ranch (1,350 MW) and Vistra’s

Texas Energy Fund project (860 MW), totaling 2,210 MW, plus at least three ERCOT queue

projects (456 MW). See PFD at 95-98.

       The PFD found that the preponderance of the evidence shows generation being actively

developed at a scale that justifies considering whether it could reduce or eliminate the need for the

unprecedented transmission expansion. See PFD at 98; Proposed FOFs 145-146. The PBRP’s

failure to test that alternative is a material deficiency. Attorney General Paxton has separately




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                         6
 raised the concern that HB 5066 does not expressly authorize 765-kV lines and that the Legislature

should review the Plan before it is implemented at this scale. See Item No. 6452.

      F. The Commission Should Not Rely on the Approval of Import Path 1 to Justify Import
         Path 2

           The PFD explained that the PBRP initiative is unlike the CREZ initiative where the

Legislature determined need for one comprehensive project, the CREZ transmission lines. No such

Legislative need determination was made for the PBRP transmission lines. Instead, under HB

5066, Applicants had to show Import Path 2 is independently necessary under the PURA § 37.056

factors.” See PFD at 55-58, 99; Proposed FOFs 128-131. The approval of Import Path 1 therefore

cannot establish need for Import Path 2.

           ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter prioritized the northern and southern

import paths for 2030 rather than central Import Path 2—sequencing the PFD described as

“essentially conceding that Import Path 2 was unnecessary through that point in time.” See PFD at

87-88. Applicants did not perform a partial-build study to justify Import Path 2 individually, and

North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) contingencies influencing ERCOT’s

regional planning are not a substitute for project-specific need. See Proposed FOFs 128-131.

            III.    KEN PAXTON, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TEXAS AND AMERICAN
                   STEWARDS OF LIBERTY, INC. HAVE IDENTIFIED FUNDAMENTAL
                   DEFICIENCIES IN THE PBRP THAT SUPPORT THE PFD’S FINDINGS

           The positions advanced by Attorney General Ken Paxton and American Stewards of

Liberty, Inc. (“ASL”) independently reinforce the PFD’s conclusions. Attorney General Paxton,

filing as amicus curiae, argues that House Bill 5066 does not expressly authorize 765-kV lines—

“[i]f the legislature wanted those lines, it would have said so” 1—and that the fiscal note included

no anticipated costs to consumers, meaning “neither the members who reviewed the bill, nor the


1
    Item No. 6452 at 12.


SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                      7
 committees that considered the bill, nor any member who voted to approve the bill, nor the

Governor, had any notice of the immense costs that the Plan as currently envisioned by PUC would

incur.” See id. at 7. No bill analysis mentions 765-kV lines; the Legislature’s interim reports

cautioned against quick adoption outside the legislative process; and the Commission’s own

representatives acknowledged that cost impacts and “guardrails” are policy questions for the

Legislature. See id. at 12. Administrative agencies “have only those powers expressly conferred

and those necessary to accomplish their duties,” 2 and the Legislature has not yet reviewed the

Plan’s scope and costs.

         ASL has consistently argued that ERCOT assumed, rather than evaluated, continued

separation between generation resources and Permian Basin load, modeling generation outside the

Permian Basin without testing whether local generation could reduce or eliminate the need for

approximately 1,255 miles of new 765-kV infrastructure. See Item Nos. 5872 and 6149. The

approximately $33 billion in proposed investment will be borne by Texas ratepayers for decades,

and the public interest favors accuracy over speed. Both the Attorney General and ASL have called

for the Commission to defer further action until the Legislature can provide guidance—a request

that is eminently reasonable given the unprecedented scale of the buildout.

                          IV.      CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF

         The PFD’s findings on need are well-supported by the evidentiary record. The ALJs

correctly concluded that Applicants failed to carry their burden under PURA § 37.056. The

Exceptions do not identify reversible error; they ask the Commission to afford dispositive weight

to ERCOT’s recommendation while ignoring material changes that have undermined the PBRP’s

foundational assumptions. The “great weight” rule does not relieve Applicants of their burden of


2
 Id. at 4 (citing State v. Jackson, 316 S.W.2d 341, 344 (Tex. 1964); Sexton v. Mount Olivet Cemetery Ass'n, 110 S.W.2d
129, 137 (Tex. App.—Austin 1986, writ ref'd)).


SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY TO PFD EXCEPTIONS                                                                        8
 proof, and it does not require the Commission to ignore material evidence of changed

circumstances.

WHEREFORE, SWG Briggs I, L.P. respectfully requests that the Commission:

       1. Deny the Exceptions of Commission Staff and Applicants Oncor Electric Delivery

          Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation on the issue of need;

       2. Sustain the PFD’s findings of fact and conclusions of law regarding the necessity of the

          Import Path 2 Projects;

       3. Deny the CCN applications for the Import Path 2 Projects; and

       4. Grant such other and further relief to which SWG Briggs I, L.P. may be justly entitled.

Date: September 9, 2026                                     Respectfully submitted,

                                                            /s/ Tyler J. Ryska

                                                            SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.
